newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Satellite phone clampdown scares Nigeria investors.
newsitem.headline: Satellite phone clampdown scares Nigeria investors.

text.p: A clampdown on private satellite communication systems by Nigeria's military rulers has cut off clients and worried investors already unsure of the government's commitment to liberalise the economy, industry officials said on Wednesday.

Communications, in which the government has promised free competition, is seen as a litmus test of how far Nigeria is willing to ignore vested interests preventing full-scale privatisation sought by business and international lenders.

"Why should anyone invest here when the rules can change just like that, and even when everything is above board the investor has no protection?" said an executive of one of the licenced Very Small Aperture Terminal satellite (V.SAT) companies, whose customers have now been cut off.
State-run Nigerian Telecommunications (NITEL) last month announced that 13 V.SAT operators, already in business, could no longer use their own operating hubs, some of which were outside Nigeria.
They were then told that henceforth they would all have to use Intelsat services, for which NITEL is the signatory and provider in Nigeria.

"The whole reason why people need V.SAT is because NITEL is incapable of meeting demand for reliability. If everything then has to pass through NITEL it makes the whole system pointless," said one V.SAT operator.
"We may as well not bother at all if we are just relegated to selling services for NITEL."

Among the V.SAT companies is Omnes Communications set up last year, a subsidiary of Omnes Worldwide, which is jointly owned by Britain's Cable and Wireless and American oil services company Schlumberger.
Other V.SAT licence holders are largely local ventures, which also aim to serve the financial sector and oil industry.

"Our clients are in pain and we are bleeding because of nearly 600 million naira ($7.3 million) investments," Randic Eruma-Gborie of V.SAT provider Sistems Worldwide told the independent Guardian newspaper.
The dire state of communications in Nigeria is the reason why business and international lenders see its privatisation as a priority.

While a NITEL programme to install digital lines has helped, phones are often cut off by heavy rain or sometimes for no obvious reason at all. Some customers complain they have to pay officials just to collect their bills.

Licences granted by the National Communications Commission, set up to oversee deregulation in the early 1990s, have still not given any private company the ability to challenge NITEL, or its breakaway mobile phone company M-TEL, across Nigeria.

Military ruler General Sani Abacha disappointed many with his 1997 budget when he shied away from privatisation, not only of telecoms but also of other priority targets like power generation and the oil industry. He said more study was needed.

Both business and the World Bank have pushed privatisation as one way to stimulate growth in Africa's most populous nation of over 100 million people, which has been in economic recession since political chaos followed the annulment of 1993 elections by a former military government.
